steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonation turns the epoxide oxygen into a good leaving group (an alcohol) and makes both ring carbons more electrophilic.

Bromide attacks anti to the C–O bond, along the axial direction, and the ring moves straight into a chair with Br and OH both axial: trans-diaxial opening (the Fürst–Plattner rule). Attack at the other carbon would have to go through a twist-boat, which costs more energy. The isomeric epoxide, with oxygen on the same face as the tert-butyl group, opens at the other carbon for the same reason. The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the drawing shows only which atoms are bonded.
Also correct arrows, but this is the minor route: attack at this carbon forms the ring first as a twist-boat, which then relaxes to a chair with Br and OH diequatorial. That path is higher in energy.

title: Trans-diaxial opening of an epoxide
subtitle: A locked ring chooses which carbon bromide attacks: the Fürst–Plattner rule

reactants.caption: 4-tert-butylcyclohexene oxide (the isomer with the oxygen on the face opposite the tert-butyl group) + HBr
hintTiers: An epoxide oxygen is a weak base, and HBr is a strong acid. What happens before any bromide attacks?
The epoxide oxygen takes the proton from HBr; the H–Br bonding pair goes to bromine. Two arrows.
Epoxide oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to the hydrogen of HBr; H–Br bond → lone pair on bromine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: HBr opens the epoxide. First, the acid.

The proton goes to the oxygen, the atom with lone pairs.

protonated-epoxide.caption: protonated epoxide + bromide
hintTiers: The tert-butyl group locks the ring. Bromide attacks anti to the oxygen, and the product must form directly as a chair with the new C–Br and the C–O bond both axial (trans-diaxial). Which carbon allows that?
With the oxygen on the face opposite the tert-butyl group, only attack at the epoxide carbon further from the tert-butyl group leads straight to a chair. Two arrows.
Bromide lone pair → new C–Br bond to the epoxide carbon further from the tert-butyl group; that carbon's C–O bond → lone pair on oxygen.
protonated-epoxide.learnerPrompt: Bromide opens the ring. Both epoxide carbons are secondary: which one does it attack?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That takes the proton back and gives the starting epoxide. Bromide's job now is to open the ring.
The oxygen carries the positive charge, but it has no empty orbital to take a pair. Bromide attacks an epoxide carbon, and a C–O bond breaks.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right carbon. It now has five bonds: which bond breaks?

mechanismSummary: The tert-butyl group holds 4-tert-butylcyclohexene oxide in one half-chair. HBr protonates the oxygen, and bromide attacks one of the two secondary epoxide carbons from the face opposite the oxygen (SN2, inversion). The carbon attacked is the one that lets the ring move directly into a chair, with the new C–Br bond and the C–O bond both axial: trans-diaxial opening. Attack at the other carbon must pass through a twist-boat, so it is minor. For the epoxide drawn (oxygen opposite the tert-butyl group) bromine ends up on the carbon further from the tert-butyl group; the other epoxide diastereomer gives the other regioisomer. The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the drawing shows only which atoms are bonded.
